extracted.intended_audience: federal agency officials, agency counsel, and administrative law practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Section-by-section guidance for federal agencies on how to comply with the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) — covering public information, rulemaking, adjudication, hearings, decisions, judicial review, and ancillary procedural requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic purposes of the Administrative Procedure Act
rubrics_metrics.description: The Administrative Procedure Act may be said to have four basic purposes: (1) To require agencies to keep the public currently informed of their organization, procedures and rules (sec. 3). (2) To provide for public participation in the rule making process (sec. 4). (3) To prescribe uniform standards for the conduct of formal rule making (sec. 4(b)) and adjudicatory proceedings (sec. 5). (4) To restate the law of judicial review (sec. 10).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four purposes form the organizing principles for agency adjustment of procedures to the Act and should be used to interpret specific section requirements in light of the Act's aims of uniformity, fairness, and preservation of effective government action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage of the APA — definition of 'agency' (sec. 2(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Agency' means each authority (whether or not within or subject to review by another agency) of the Government of the United States other than Congress, the courts, or the governments of the possessions, Territories, or the District of Columbia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'agency' is to be read broadly to include constituent units and subdivisions that have final authority (e.g., Social Security Administration). The definition focuses on the 'authority' vested in persons or boards rather than formal organizational labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemptions from the operation of the Act (section 2(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain agencies and functions are excluded from the Act's operation (except section 3): (1) agencies composed of representatives of the parties to disputes; (2) courts-martial and military commissions; (3) military or naval authority exercised in the field in time of war or in occupied territory; and (4) functions which by law expire on termination of hostilities or before July 1, 1947, and certain specified statutes (Selective Service, Contract Settlement, Surplus Property, Sugar Control Extension, Veterans' Emergency Housing, Housing and Rent Acts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exemptions are to be considered separately and specifically; when in doubt agencies should note the exception's scope (temporary functions remain exempt even if they continue after combat). Section 3 (public information) still applies to most exempted bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions — 'Rule' and 'Rule making' (section 2(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Rule' means the whole or any part of any agency statement of general or particular applicability and future effect designed to implement, interpret, or prescribe law or policy or to describe the organization, procedure, or practice requirements of any agency. 'Rule making' means agency process for the formulation, amendment, or repeal of a rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'rule' is broad: it includes substantive, interpretative, organizational and procedural rules; it covers rules of general applicability and those applying to a class or single person, provided they have future effect (e.g., approval of a corporate reorganization may be rule making).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions — 'Order' and 'Adjudication' (section 2(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Order' means the whole or any part of the final disposition (whether affirmative, negative, injunctive, or declaratory) of any agency in any matter other than rule making but including licensing. 'Adjudication' means agency process for the formulation of an order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjudication is largely residual ('other than rule making') and typically concerns past or present rights and liabilities (e.g., unfair labor practice proceedings, benefit claims, licensing decisions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of 'rule' vs. licensing/adjudication — practical construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Proceedings that fit specific categories enumerated in section 2(c) (e.g., determining rates for the future) are rule making rather than adjudication; listing in section 2(c) is illustrative, not exclusive. The purposes of the underlying statute and the factors the agency must weigh are relevant to classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify proceedings by their legislative/policy character: actions that regulate future conduct or implement policy are typically rule making; those resolving past conduct or individual entitlements are adjudicatory. This classification affects which procedural provisions (e.g., sections 4, 5, 7, 8) apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 3 — Public information: separate statement and publication requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 3 directs each agency to 'separately state and currently publish in the Federal Register' its organization, procedures and substantive rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Materials must be published under separate and appropriate headings (organization, procedures, substantive rules) but agencies should avoid impractical fragmentation; cross-references between sections are permissible (e.g., procedure statement may refer to substantive rules for application forms). All materials issued under section 3(a) should be included in the Code of Federal Regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 3(a)(1) — Description of organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must separately state and publish descriptions of their central and field organization including delegations by the agency of final authority and the established places at which, and methods whereby, the public may secure information or make submittals or requests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only delegations of final authority need be listed and should be identified by office/title (not necessarily individual names). Field offices should be listed with locations and functions; state whether field offices may issue interpretative/advisory opinions and whether such opinions are subject to central review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 3(a)(2) — Statement of procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must separately state the general course and method by which their functions are channeled and determined, including the nature and requirements of all formal or informal procedures available as well as forms and instructions as to the scope and contents of all papers, reports, or examinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe the procedures by which rule making, adjudication, and program administration (loans, grants, benefits) are carried out. Section 3 does not freeze procedures; it does not require more formality than previously prevailing. Where doubt exists whether a matter affects the public, publish it in the Federal Register unless it requires secrecy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 3(a)(3) — Publication of substantive rules, policy statements and interpretations
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication in the Federal Register is required of substantive rules (and statements of general policy and interpretations formulated and adopted by the agency for the guidance of the public) issued on or after the section's effective date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substantive rules and interpretative guidance should be drafted in Federal Register-compatible form; agencies may consult the Division of the Federal Register for assistance. Section 3 is prospective in operation (no requirement to republish materials issued prior to effective date if previously published).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions to Section 3 — 'secrecy in the public interest'
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 3 does not require publication 'to the extent' that any function of the United States requires secrecy in the public interest (e.g., confidential law enforcement operations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency must determine the scope of secrecy; where only part of a function requires secrecy the rest must be published. The exception is not limited to investigatory functions — e.g., Comptroller of the Currency may issue confidential rules to banks where publicity would harm public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions to Section 3 — 'matters solely relating to internal management'
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 3 excludes 'any matter relating solely to the internal management of an agency' (e.g., personnel and budget procedures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internal management includes intra-agency and internal Federal management functions (e.g., many Bureau of the Budget functions). When in doubt whether a matter is internal, publish it in the Federal Register unless secrecy applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 4 — Rule making: applicability only to substantive rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 4 (apart from 4(d)) is applicable only to substantive rules, i.e., rules issued pursuant to statutory authority to implement statutory power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretative, organizational, and procedural rules are 'rules' under section 2(c) but the formal requirements of section 4 apply only to substantive rules; agencies must determine whether a rule is 'substantive' to know if notice-and-comment requirements attach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 4(a) — Notice requirement and contents of notice
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 4(a) requires notice in rule making; the manual discusses 'Contents of notice' as a required element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although this manual's excerpt lists 'Contents of notice' as a topic, the agency should ensure notices adequately describe the subject matter, legal authority, issues posed, and opportunity for public comment; the contents should inform interested persons how to participate effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of notice and public procedure for 'good cause'
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 4 permits omission of notice and public procedure when good cause exists for doing so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good-cause omissions should be narrowly construed and justified in the record; emergency or imperative public need may justify immediate final rules but agencies must explain why notice-and-comment would be impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 4(b) — Procedures: informal and formal rule making; publication of procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 4(b) contemplates both informal rule making (notice-and-comment) and formal rule making (on the record, with trial-type procedures) and requires agencies to publish their procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should publish the procedures they follow for rule making. Where statute requires formal rule making, agencies must follow the evidentiary and hearing processes appropriate to an on-the-record proceeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 4(c) — Effective dates
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 4(c) addresses effective dates of rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should follow the Act's provisions and customary practices regarding when rules become effective (the manual discusses effective-date rules and any statutory exceptions); ensure the record supports any deviation from normal effective-date rules for necessity or urgency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 4(d) — Petitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 4(d) covers petitions related to rule making (listed in table of contents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should provide for petitions for rule making and clear standards for their consideration; where a petition is denied the denial may be an exercise of discretion unreviewable by courts in some circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 5 — Adjudication: general procedural requirements and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 5 prescribes uniform standards for adjudicatory proceedings required by statute to be made on the record after opportunity for an agency hearing; it sets out general scope, exempted adjudications, and specific procedural rules (notice, responsive pleading, hearing procedures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must follow the Act's adjudicatory requirements for those proceedings statutorily required to be on the record, but exemptions and special classes of cases (e.g., inspections, tests) may not be covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 5(a) — Notice and responsive pleading in adjudications
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 5(a) requires notice in adjudications and provides for responsive pleadings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notices should provide sufficient specification of charges or issues so parties can prepare responsive pleadings; agencies should ensure procedural fairness by permitting timely responses and appropriate forms of pleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 5(b) — Adjudicatory procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 5(b) sets forth procedural protections and processes to be followed in adjudication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should follow the adjudicatory due-process-type protections indicated (opportunity to present evidence, cross-examination as needed, record-based decision making) and observe limits where statute or practice provides alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 5(c) — Separation of functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 5(c) requires separation of investigative/prosecutorial and decisionmaking functions; the hearing officer who presides is generally required to prepare the initial or recommended decision, and agency officers who performed investigative or prosecuting functions may not participate in the decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reflects the adjudicatory character of the proceeding; exceptions exist (notably for rule making and certain licensing) and must be applied as the statute allows. Agencies must design procedures to avoid participation by conflicted staff in final decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 5(d) — Declaratory orders
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 5(d) covers declaratory orders as a form of agency adjudicatory disposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may provide procedures for declaratory orders; ensure the record and opportunity to be heard are adequate to support declaratory relief to be consistent with the Act's requirements where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 6(a) — Appearance: formal and informal appearance; practice before agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 6(a) addresses appearance, formal and informal, and practice before agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should define who may appear, procedures for formal appearance, and standards for practicing before the agency. They should publish such practice rules under section 3 where they affect the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 6(b) and 6(c) — Investigations and subpoenas
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 6(b) covers investigative powers; section 6(c) addresses subpoenas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies exercising investigatory or subpoena powers must observe statutory limits and provide sufficient procedural safeguards; guidance and examples in the manual should be consulted when implementing investigative procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 6(d) — Denials
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 6(d) treats denials (e.g., denial of requests or forms of relief) as an ancillary matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should make denial procedures transparent and publish any rules governing denials that affect the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 7(a) — Presiding officers (hearing officers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 7(a) addresses presiding officers: the hearing may be before a hearing officer appointed for that purpose or an agency member; agencies may appoint substantial numbers of hearing officers, possibly full-time, with appointments subject to Civil Service considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners/hearing officers are to be qualified and may be appointed subject to civil service; agencies must consider rotation, workload, compensation (Civil Service Commission prescribes), and that examiners serve only as examiners except in limited circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 7(b) — Hearing powers and delegation
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 7(b) allows the agency to delegate any of the enumerated powers to a hearing officer; the enumeration of powers is not intended to be exclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may grant hearing officers broad powers as needed, consistent with the Act; delegation should be described in agency procedures and organizations statements under section 3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 7(c) — Evidence rules and burden of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: The proponent of a rule or order has the burden of proof (subject to statutory exceptions). Parties have the right to cross-examine as necessary for a full and true disclosure of the facts. Agencies may accept technical written reports and other non-oral evidence where reasonable, and may dispense with oral evidence in enumerated instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may receive any evidence deemed relevant, reliable, and probative; they should ensure procedures for cross-examination where credibility/demeanor matter. Courts reviewing agency findings are governed by the 'substantial evidence' standard (section 10(e)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 7(d) — Record for decision and official notice
rubrics_metrics.description: The transcript of testimony and exhibits, together with all papers and requests filed in the proceeding, shall constitute the exclusive record for decision in cases covered by section 7. The agency may take official notice of material facts not appearing in the record, provided it states such notice in the record or decision and affords parties a timely opportunity to show the contrary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must preserve the hearing record for decision; when taking official notice, ensure parties have a chance to rebut. The 'exclusive record' requirement is tied to statutory on-the-record adjudications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 8(a) — Who decides; initial, recommended and final decisions; agency review
rubrics_metrics.description: Either the agency or a subordinate hearing officer may make the initial decision. The initial decision of the hearing officer, in the absence of appeal, becomes the decision of the agency. Upon review the agency may limit review to questions of law, or to whether findings are supported by substantial evidence or the weight of evidence; it may also make new findings on the record or on new evidence, remand, or adopt other procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When agency makes initial decision without presiding, a recommended decision by the presiding officer is generally required unless exceptions apply (rule making, initial licenses, or imperative timely execution). Agencies must give parties opportunity to present contentions to the agency before final decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 8(b) — Opportunity to submit proposed findings and exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to each recommended, initial, or tentative decision, parties shall have a timely opportunity to submit proposed findings and conclusions; prior to decision on agency review parties may submit exceptions to initial/recommended/tentative decisions. Subject to agency rules, such submissions may be oral where adequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should publish rules on timing and format of proposed findings and exceptions; permit oral presentation when sufficient for fairness and practicality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 9(a) — Sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 9(a) declares established law concerning agency sanctions (e.g., enforcement powers) and is intended to declare the existing law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies exercising sanctioning powers must follow established legal standards and ensure procedural safeguards where penalties may be imposed; section 9(b) codifies licensing practices and standards for licenses, suspensions, revocation, and renewal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 9(b) — Licenses: application, suspension, revocation, renewal
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 9(b) covers licenses: applications for licenses, suspension or revocation, and renewal of licenses. The second sentence of subsection (b) is not intended to apply to temporary licenses issued pending determination of applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Licensing proceedings may be adjudicatory; agencies should set procedures for applications and for handling suspensions/renewals consistent with statutory requirements and the Act's protective provisions where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 10(a) — Right to judicial review
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person suffering legal wrong because of any agency action, or adversely affected or aggrieved by such action within the meaning of any relevant statute, shall be entitled to judicial review of such action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The scope of who is 'aggrieved' is governed by existing case law (e.g., Alabama Power, Sanders Bros.). Agencies should assume that persons adversely affected may seek review unless statute plainly precludes it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 10(b) — Form and venue of action
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a specific statutory method is provided for review, that procedure shall be used; if no such procedure exists or if it is inadequate, other remedies (injunctions, declaratory judgments, habeas corpus) are available. The validity of agency action may also be raised in enforcement proceedings unless prior exclusive opportunity to contest has been provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should be mindful of statutory review schemes and the adequacy of those schemes; if an agency provides an adequate exclusive review procedure courts are less likely to permit alternative challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 10(c) — Acts reviewable and exhaustion of administrative remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 10(c) states the acts which are reviewable under section 10 and makes clear that exhaustion of administrative remedies as to finality is intended only (1) where expressly required by statute or (2) where agency rules require appeal to superior authority before action is final for judicial review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should publish their internal appeal rules; parties ordinarily must await final agency action unless statute or agency rules provide otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 10(d) — Interim relief
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may grant interim relief (e.g., stay of enforcement) pending judicial review where necessary to prevent irreparable injury; this may modify prior common-law understandings in some contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should consider the possibility of interim relief and preserve the record of irreparable injury and public interest considerations when enforcement actions are taken that could be stayed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 10(e) — Scope of judicial review: substantial evidence and harmless error
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 10(e) declares existing law concerning scope of review: courts apply the 'substantial evidence' rule in reviewing agency factfinding. The statute adopts the rule that error is not fatal unless prejudicial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency factfinding should be supported by relevant, reliable, and probative evidence; agencies need not treat every procedural error as fatal provided the error was not prejudicial to the outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 11 — Appointment, compensation and tenure of examiners (hearing officers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 11 provides for appointment, compensation, and tenure of examiners who will preside over hearings and render decisions pursuant to sections 7 and 8. Examiners are to be appointed subject to civil service to the extent not inconsistent with the Act, be used in rotation where practicable, and be removable only for good cause established and determined by the Civil Service Commission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should adopt appointment and rotation procedures consistent with Civil Service guidance; examiners generally serve only as examiners but may be assigned limited additional duties not inconsistent with their hearing role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 12 — Construction and effect of the Act
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 12 indicates the Act supplements constitutional and legal requirements and that no subsequent legislation shall be held to supersede or modify the provisions of this Act except to the extent such later legislation does so expressly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Act should be interpreted broadly as expressing general standards of wide applicability unless subsequent legislation clearly provides otherwise; agencies and courts should attempt to apply the Act consistently with other statutory and constitutional obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive vs. interpretative/organizational/procedural rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition of 'rule' in section 2(c) is not limited to substantive rules but embraces interpretative, organizational and procedural rules as well, but section 4's formal requirements apply only to substantive rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must distinguish which class a statement falls into because the procedural obligations (e.g., notice-and-comment) differ; interpretative or internal procedural statements may not trigger section 4 but may still require publication under section 3 unless exempt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of proceedings: policy factors and practical consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an agency proceeding is rule making or adjudication depends on whether the action regulates future conduct and involves policy (rule making) versus determining past/present rights and liabilities with accusatory flavor (adjudication).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification has practical consequences: participation rules, who writes the initial decision, permissible staff consultations, and whether formal on-the-record procedures apply. Agencies should analyze the statute's purpose and the considerations required in decisionmaking to classify proceedings correctly.
